# Reference profile

Use this page to run CALIBER as the reference deployment: one supported shape that **refuses to start**
while any of the settings below is unsafe. It is the deployment the EGI reference architecture's claims
(governed action, safe restart, evidence) are made about; `docs/architecture/adr/0001-reference-profile.md`
defines the whole shape, and this page lists what the process itself enforces today.

## Turn it on

Set `CALIBER_PROFILE=reference`. The default, `development`, starts with whatever is configured and behaves
exactly as before. Under `reference`, `create_app` checks the configuration **before** it opens the database
or creates the bootstrap account, so a refused start leaves nothing behind, and it lists **every** violation
at once:

```text
reference profile refused (2 violations):
- database_url is a SQLite file; set CALIBER_DATABASE_URL=<a PostgreSQL URL> for the reference profile
- csrf_enabled is false; set CALIBER_CSRF_ENABLED=true for the reference profile
```

An unknown profile name is a configuration error. `GET /ajax-api/2.0/mlflow/caliber/readiness` carries a
`profile` field, so an operator can see which rules the running process was started under.

## What it requires

| violation code | setting | environment variable | required | why |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `sqlite_database` | `database_url` | `CALIBER_DATABASE_URL` | a PostgreSQL URL | SQLite allows one writer and the reference profile's recovery and ownership guarantees need row locks and real transactions. |
| `csrf_disabled` | `csrf_enabled` | `CALIBER_CSRF_ENABLED` | true (with CALIBER_CSRF_SIGNING_SECRET set) | Without CSRF protection a page the approver visits can submit an approval for them. |
| `dev_fallback_enabled` | `auth_dev_fallback_enabled` | `CALIBER_AUTH_DEV_FALLBACK_ENABLED` | false | The no-header fallback makes an unauthenticated request an admin. |
| `insecure_bootstrap` | `auth_bootstrap_allow_insecure_default` | `CALIBER_AUTH_BOOTSTRAP_ALLOW_INSECURE_DEFAULT` | false | It allows an `admin`/`admin` bootstrap account when no password is set and the session cookie is not marked secure. |
| `trusted_header_without_proxy_secret` | `auth_mode` | `CALIBER_AUTH_TRUSTED_PROXY_SECRET_ENV` | `session`, or `trusted_header` with the name of the variable that holds the proxy secret | Trusting an identity header without a proxy secret lets any client claim any identity. |
| `egress_policy_disabled` | `egress_policy_enabled` | `CALIBER_EGRESS_POLICY_ENABLED` | true | The egress policy is what stops a tool or webhook from reaching internal addresses. |
| `mcp_insecure_http` | `mcp_allow_insecure_http` | `CALIBER_MCP_ALLOW_INSECURE_HTTP` | false | Plain-HTTP MCP servers send tool calls and results in the clear. |
| `self_approval_allowed` | `approval_allow_self_approval` | `CALIBER_APPROVAL_ALLOW_SELF_APPROVAL` | false | The account that started a run could approve its own protected action. |
| `apply_distinct_approver_disabled` | `apply_require_distinct_approver` | `CALIBER_APPLY_REQUIRE_DISTINCT_APPROVER` | true | The account that requested a refinement job could apply its own candidate to production, and a job with no recorded requester could be applied unreviewed. |
| `memory_inference_enabled` | `memory_infer` | `CALIBER_MEMORY_INFER` | false while CALIBER_MEMORY_ENABLED is true | LLM-inferred memory writes create durable, free-form facts nobody owns; the owned memory lifecycle does not exist yet. |
| `fault_barriers_enabled` | `fault_barriers` | `CALIBER_FAULT_BARRIERS` | unset | An armed fault barrier makes the process exit on purpose; it exists only for scenario tests. |

The messages in the refusal name the setting and the variable to change. The table is checked by
`caliber/tests/test_profile.py`: a rule that is not listed here, or a row without a rule, fails the build.

## What it also does at runtime

Beyond refusing to start, the reference profile **bounds every request body**: a body above
`CALIBER_REFERENCE_MAX_BODY_BYTES` (default 1 MiB) is answered `413` with
`{"reason": "request_too_large", "max_bytes": N}`, whether the client declared a large `Content-Length` or
streamed the body without one (or understated it). The check is the outermost layer, so an oversized request
is refused before authentication, CSRF or routing reads it. A request at exactly the limit is accepted, and the
development profile installs no limit.

Two kinds of request have a limit of their own, because their routes accept more than 1 MiB. The larger limit
applies; the default is never lower than a route's own:

| request | limit | setting |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `multipart/form-data` (skill zips, attachments, workspace imports, storage objects) | 256 MiB | `CALIBER_REFERENCE_MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES`; raise it together with `CALIBER_WORKFLOW_STORAGE_MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES` (250 MiB), which each route still enforces, tighter, afterwards |
| the GitHub webhook route | `CALIBER_GITHUB_WEBHOOK_MAX_BODY_BYTES` (2 MiB) | the route's own setting; the global 1 MiB never lowers it |

A refusal carries `x-request-id` (the caller's, or one generated) and writes one warning log line naming the
method, path and size. The body is refused, not drained, so a client that keeps sending a very large body may see
a connection reset rather than the `413`.

## Governed webhook and API-request nodes

Manifest-backed `webhook` and `api_request` nodes use the registered private `http` effect backend. Before a request
is sent, the runtime records an immutable proposal containing the node occurrence, URL, method, headers, timeout and
body. Dispatch then rechecks the exact bound approval and the captured `execution-owner` lease in one transaction,
emits the durable dispatch event, and only then calls the private transport. The path does not call a public CALIBER
route or recursively invoke the OpenAPI execution surface. Egress is checked before the proposal is submitted and by
the default client at connection time.

The generic HTTP backend cannot assume that every endpoint supports durable idempotency or a lookup-by-key API. It
therefore emits `Idempotency-Key` from the proposal's stable logical key, but requires the runtime caller to provide an
authoritative receipt verifier for the endpoint. The verifier must read the downstream's own state and return receipt
facts matching the proposal's connector, resource, intent hash and attempt. A missing verifier, missing exact approval or
missing lease is refused before transport; a response that cannot be verified does not become `committed` and remains
recoverable as an unknown effect. The platform makes no universal exactly-once claim for arbitrary HTTP services.

A manifest-backed plan without this governed context is refused rather than falling back to the raw sender. Legacy plans
without a workflow manifest retain the existing `_perform_guarded_effect` ledger behavior and do not create an effect
proposal. The runtime integration that owns a run must bind the context with the run id, exact approval provider, live
execution-owner lease and endpoint-specific verifier; no new environment variable, SDK route or migration is required.

## Governed registered tools (B04.3)

A workflow `tool` node that names a registered Python tool is routed by the tool's **registry row**, read from the
database for the tool being run: its name, owner, version, module, callable and declared side-effect level. The
manifest binding, an exported bundle and the model do not decide it (`IRToolBinding` and `ToolRegistryEntry` carry
no owner, so there is nothing in them to forge). A plan is governed when it is wired to the registry (an identity reader) or to an authority (a governed context); the
table below lists every place the runtime builds a plan and which it is. OpenAPI bindings are routed the same way by
[Governed OpenAPI tools](#governed-openapi-tools-b044), and MCP bindings (B04.5) keep their own path.

| the registry row is | the tool node |
| --- | --- |
| a CALIBER built-in (`@caliber`, version `1.0`, its own module and callable) the protected-effect inventory refuses (EP-055: `read_text_file`, `list_folder_files`, `grep_files`, `regex_search`; `sandbox_python`) | refused before it is bound or called: `registered tool '<name>' refused: unsupported_effect_path`; nothing is recorded |
| a CALIBER built-in classified `read` (and declared `read`) | runs inline, as before |
| any other CALIBER built-in | proposed, approved and dispatched at the inventory class (or the declared class when stricter) |
| a row that reuses a built-in's reserved name without being the seed's own row, a tool with no readable row, or an unrecognised declared level | classified `irreversible_write`, the fail-closed class, and dispatched; never inline |
| an administrator-registered tool declared `read` | runs inline, as before |
| an administrator-registered tool declared `write` or `external_action` | proposed, approved and dispatched; the proposal records `irreversible_write` because the inventory does not list it; the recorded class is always the stricter of the inventory's class and the class the row's declared level implies |
| a row whose module, callable or backend differs from the binding | refused: `registered tool '<name>' does not match its registry row` |

A protected call follows the same boundary as the governed HTTP nodes: the runtime records an immutable proposal
(`connector: registered_tool`, resource `registered-tool/<name>/<version>`, the tool's arguments and input), asks the
run's authorization provider for the exact approval and the captured `execution-owner` lease, and `dispatch` rechecks
both in one transaction, consumes the approval and writes the dispatch event **before** the private `registered_tool`
backend calls the bound tool. The tool is called with the arguments **recorded in the proposal**, not with what the
caller still holds, and never retried (the binding's `max_retries` is ignored for a governed call): a tool that raises or
times out leaves the proposal `unknown` for the reconciler. A local callable has no downstream key to replay, so the
platform makes no exactly-once claim; it guarantees at most one claim per logical effect, and re-executing a finished
node does not call the tool again. The `registered_tool` backend is a pinned entry of the reference profile's trusted
connector table (`REFERENCE_CONNECTORS`): its implementation, capability record (no key to replay, no lookup) and settings
(`invoker`, `receipt_verifier`) are admitted, and it accepts the risks `write_not_exactly_once` and
`key_retention_unconfirmed` by name. As for HTTP, the run's context must supply an authoritative `receipt_verifier`; a
response it cannot verify does not become `committed`.

Every refusal is a `ToolExecutionError` carrying a stable code and no argument, input or tool output:

```text
registered tool effect proposal refused: bad_field              # arguments or input too large or not plain JSON
registered tool effect authorization was not granted           # no exact approval: the proposal stays `proposed`
registered tool effect authorization failed: ValueError         # the provider raised; only the type is reported
registered tool effect dispatch refused: proposal_not_approved  # not approved, or the node already ran
registered tool effect did not commit: ambiguous:unclassified_error  # the tool raised: effect unknown, not retried
'tool_node' requires a governed effect context to run protected registered tool 'open_ticket'
registered tool 'open_ticket' identity could not be read: ConnectionError
```

Recovery: a `proposed` effect needs an exact approval, after which the run can be resumed or resubmitted (the proposal
is reused for the same node occurrence, so the tool still runs once); an `unknown` effect is settled by the reconciler
(B05) or an operator, never by re-running the node; a manifest-backed deployment whose run owner has not bound a
governed context must keep protected registered tools out of its workflows, because it refuses them (read-class tools
are unaffected). Every construction site of a runtime plan (`RuntimePlan(`) in the code, and what it does with a protected registry tool:

| plan built by | used for | registry reader | protected registry tool |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `promoter.build_plan` | worker runs, synchronous version runs, sub-workflows, Aria previews | bound | refused until a governed context is bound (#1051); a preview stubs it |
| `refinement._replay` (via `orchestrator/workflow_stages.py::run_workflow_eval`) | candidate evaluation | bound by the stage | refused (typed, nothing recorded); read-class tools run |
| `calibration._replay_calibration_manifest` (via `evaluate_workflow_calibration_candidates` in the stage) | calibration replay | bound by the stage | refused; read-class tools run |
| `promoter` deploy-gate replay | release gate evaluation | none, but `preview=True` | stubbed, never run for real |
| `export_runtime.execute_exported_workflow` | standalone exports | none (no registry to read) | **not governed**: called directly |
| a caller that builds a plan itself (tests, SDK embedding) | any | none unless it passes one | **not governed**: called directly |

The two evaluation replays used to call a candidate manifest's write tools for real (found in review of B04.3); they now refuse
them, so a workflow whose protected tool must be exercised by an evaluation or calibration needs that tool replaced by a
read-class stand-in until the replay can run under a governed context (#1051). The module-import paths stay inventory rows
EP-015, EP-016 and EP-019, refused by #774.

Two limits. An administrator-registered tool declared `read` is trusted as read-class: its declared level is part of the
definition the deployment bundle pins and re-verifies before a run (`deployment_bundle.tool_snapshot`), but the platform
does not observe what its code does, so register a tool that writes with `write` or `external_action`. And model-chosen tool
calls inside an agent step and MCP tools are not routed by this change (B04.5 to B04.7); OpenAPI tool nodes are routed by
[Governed OpenAPI tools](#governed-openapi-tools-b044).

No migration, no new setting and no new route; rolling back is reverting the change (a `registered_tool` proposal
already recorded remains readable and reconcilable).

## Governed OpenAPI tools (B04.4)

A workflow `tool` node bound to a tool published from an OpenAPI integration (`execution_backend: openapi_http`) is routed
by the tool's **registry row**, as a registered Python tool is, and by the operation that row selects. Two things the
registry holds decide the class, and the stricter wins: the row's declared `side_effect_level` and the **method** of the
operation its own `backend_config` describes (a tool pack's operation is chosen by the call's `operation` input from the
row's list of bound operations, never from the binding). The manifest binding, an exported bundle and the model decide
nothing: the binding's `backend_config` and `input_schema` must equal the row's, or the node is refused.

| the row and its operation | the tool node |
| --- | --- |
| `GET`, `HEAD` or `OPTIONS`, declared `read` | runs inline, as before: no proposal, no approval |
| `GET`, `HEAD` or `OPTIONS`, declared `write` or `external_action` | proposed, approved and dispatched (the declared level floors the class) |
| `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH` or `DELETE`, whatever the level (an under-declared `read` included) | proposed, approved and dispatched: a method that is not a read method is at least a `reversible_write` |
| a built-in's reserved name, or an unrecognised level | classified `irreversible_write` and dispatched; never inline |
| a tool with no readable row, a row that is not an OpenAPI tool, or an operation the row does not bind | refused before anything is recorded or sent |
| a binding whose configuration or schema differs from the row | refused: `registered tool '<name>' does not match its registry row` |
| a protected call in a plan with no governed context, or replaced by an injected callable | refused: nothing is recorded or sent |
| a protected method reaching the **public** OpenAPI entry from anywhere else (an export, a model-chosen call, Aria, an ungoverned plan) | refused before anything is prepared or sent: `unsupported_effect_path` |

The proposal (`connector: openapi-http`, always recorded `irreversible_write`, because the inventory does not list a registered
tool) holds the resource `openapi/<METHOD> <server><path template>`, built from the row, and the arguments
`{"tool", "version", "input"}`. Dispatch rechecks the exact approval and the captured `execution-owner` lease in one
transaction, consumes the approval and writes the dispatch event **before** the private `openapi_http` backend sends. That
backend sends through the **private raw transport**: it rebuilds the request from the row and the
**recorded** arguments, requires the result to be the recorded resource (method, server and path) and sends nothing
otherwise, so what is sent is what the approver saw, and it can never reach the dispatcher or the public entry again.

**The public entry reads; the private transport sends.** `execute_openapi_http_tool` (and `bind_openapi_http_tool`, which wraps
it) is the public entry of the OpenAPI executor. It sends only an operation whose method reads (`GET`, `HEAD`, `OPTIONS`):
any other method is refused with `unsupported_effect_path` before the input is validated, a secret is resolved or anything is
sent, so no caller of it can perform a protected effect without a recorded, approved proposal. The method is read from the
tool's **configuration** (a pack's operation is chosen by the input), never from a claim. A configuration that resolves to no
operation gets the executor's ordinary configuration refusal instead. The send itself is the module-private `_send_raw`, which
only three modules may name: the dispatcher's private backends (document request and `openapi_http`) and the operator's draft
preview route (EP-033, exempt: a human fires one call, gated by `allow_in_preview`). It never calls the public entry, so a
dispatched effect cannot re-enter the dispatcher or the public path. `tests/test_effect_path_matrix.py` fails when any other
production module names `_send_raw` (`test_the_private_raw_transport_is_named_only_by_pinned_modules`) or the public entry
(`test_the_raw_openapi_executor_is_named_only_by_pinned_callers`). A read-method tool is still classified by the registry row
**before** it reaches the public entry (a `GET` declared `write` is dispatched), and Aria checks a tool's declared level itself.

**Everything that can be refused without sending is refused before the proposal is recorded**, so no approval is requested or
spent for a call that cannot be made: the input against the row's schema, the server (a plain `http(s)` origin with no
credentials, query or fragment, because its text is persisted in the resource), the egress policy for the request URL and for an
OAuth token URL, an unsupported auth kind, a caller-supplied idempotency key and a conflicting precondition. No secret is
resolved and nothing is sent at that point; the transport applies the egress policy again when it connects.

**Keys, preconditions and retries.**

- When the row binds an idempotency key header, **the platform owns the key**: the transport sends the proposal's stable
  logical key, and an `idempotency_key` input or a `header_params` entry for that header is refused
  (`openapi_key_override_refused`), never sent next to it.
- When the row binds a precondition header (for example `If-Match`), the `expected_resource_version` input and a
  `header_params` entry must agree (`openapi_precondition_conflict`). The value is recorded **once**, as the proposal's
  `expected_resource_version` (so the approval is bound to it and the approver's check compares it with the current version),
  and the transport sends it as the bound header. A recorded precondition the row cannot send is refused, never dropped.
- The transport retries only when the request really carries an emitted key: a row with no key header is sent **once**, even
  for a method the executor would otherwise retry (`PUT`, `DELETE`). With a key, the executor's own bounded retry (the row's
  `max_attempts`, at most 5) repeats the same key **within one dispatch**. The dispatcher does not redrive an ambiguous
  effect after that dispatch, and the binding's `max_retries` is ignored for a governed call. The in-dispatch retry is an
  **accepted risk**, not a guarantee: the capability record leaves key scope and retention unconfirmed, so a downstream that
  does not honour the key can commit twice. Leave `max_attempts` at 1 unless the downstream is known to replay a key.

**Headers, and what is stored.** `header_params` may not set a method-override header (`X-HTTP-Method-Override`,
`X-HTTP-Method`, `X-Method-Override`) or a framing or hop-by-hop header (`Host`, `Content-Length`, `Content-Encoding`,
`Transfer-Encoding`, `Connection`, `Keep-Alive`, `Proxy-Connection`, `Proxy-Authorization`, `TE`, `Trailer`, `Upgrade`,
`Expect`; case-insensitive): classification uses the row's method, and a downstream that honours an override would turn a read into a
write. The check applies to **every** call of the executor, an inline `GET` included, and is refused as
`openapi_header_forbidden` (a governed call, before the proposal) or as an executor error that names no header (an inline call).
It does not cover a method override carried in a query parameter or a body field a particular downstream might honour. The
input is recorded **verbatim**: `body`, `header_params`, `query_params` and `path_params` are stored in the proposal's
`args.input` (`caliber_effect_proposals`) and shown to the approver, so **credentials belong in the row's `auth_binding`
(a secret reference resolved at send time), never in the call's input**. The proposal never records the auth binding.

**What an answer proves.** The `openapi-http` capability record promises nothing about a downstream: no key scope or
retention, no lookup by key, no documented rejection status. So a 2xx is a claim that the run's authoritative
`receipt_verifier` must confirm (an unconfirmed claim stays `unknown`), and every other answer, a 4xx included, is
`unknown` rather than `failed`. A connection dropped or timed out after the downstream committed is `unknown`: the node does
not run again, the reconciler has no lookup binding for this connector and leaves it (`not_bound`), and only the verifier, a
receipt callback or an operator can settle it. The connector is a pinned entry of `REFERENCE_CONNECTORS` (backend kind
`openapi_http`, settings `operation` and `receipt_verifier`, accepted risks `write_not_exactly_once` and
`key_retention_unconfirmed`).

Every refusal is a `ToolExecutionError` with a stable code and no argument, input, header, URL or response body:

```text
OpenAPI effect proposal refused: openapi_egress_blocked         # the request or token URL fails the egress policy
OpenAPI effect proposal refused: openapi_input_invalid          # input breaks the row's schema, or a path parameter is missing
OpenAPI effect proposal refused: openapi_key_override_refused   # a caller-supplied idempotency key for a row that binds one
OpenAPI effect proposal refused: openapi_precondition_conflict  # If-Match and expected_resource_version disagree, or are blank
OpenAPI effect proposal refused: openapi_config_invalid         # the row's server or path cannot be used (credentials, query, scheme)
OpenAPI effect proposal refused: openapi_auth_unsupported       # the row binds an auth kind the executor does not support
OpenAPI effect proposal refused: openapi_header_forbidden       # header_params sets a method-override, framing or hop-by-hop header
OpenAPI tool 'tickets' refused: openapi_operation_unresolved    # a pack operation the row does not bind
OpenAPI tool 'tickets' refused: unsupported_effect_path         # no readable OpenAPI row for the tool
unsupported_effect_path: a protected OpenAPI call is sent only by the effect dispatcher   # a non-read method at the public entry
OpenAPI effect authorization was not granted                    # no exact approval: the proposal stays `proposed`
OpenAPI effect dispatch refused: proposal_not_approved          # not approved, or the node already ran
OpenAPI effect did not commit: ambiguous:http_503               # unknown: the answer proves nothing, nothing is resent
OpenAPI effect did not commit: receipt_unverified               # a 2xx the verifier could not confirm: unknown
'tool_node' requires a governed effect context to run protected OpenAPI tool 'open_ticket'
```

Recovery: a refusal before the proposal needs the input, the row or the egress allowlist corrected (nothing was recorded). A
`proposed` effect needs an exact approval, after which the run can be resumed (the proposal is reused for the same node
occurrence). An `unknown` effect is settled by the receipt verifier, a receipt callback or an operator (see the
[recovery runbook](m-65-recovery-runbook.md)), never by running the node again.

**After the approval.** The backend rebuilds the request from the row and the recorded arguments and checks it again,
the egress policy included. Any failure at that point (a recorded proposal that is not the row's operation, or a destination
that **stopped** passing the egress policy since the proposal, a transient DNS or allowlist change included) sends nothing and
settles the proposal `failed` with the reason `not_sent`; the dispatch's internal refusal code is not surfaced, and **the
approval is already consumed**: ask for a new proposal (run the node again after fixing the cause).

**Not routed through the dispatcher, and what they can do now (B04.4b).** Model-chosen tool calls inside an agent step (B04.6,
#768), the Aria assistant's published-tool call (inventory EP-034: there is no workflow run to propose into; owned by #1063),
standalone exports and plans a caller builds itself (#1051: `build_plan` binds the registry reader but no governed context, so a
deployed workflow's **protected** OpenAPI nodes are refused until #1051 binds one; read-class `GET` nodes still run) all reach
the **public** entry, which refuses a protected method with `unsupported_effect_path`. So none of them can perform an OpenAPI
write any more: they can read, and a write needs the governed route above. This is a behavior change for an Aria deployment in
`build` mode with `auto_all` or `full_autonomy` approval, which no longer offers a write or external-action tool to the model
(it could only fail), for a tool declared `read` whose operation is a `POST` (refused rather than sent), and for a standalone
export whose tool writes. The operator's draft preview route (EP-033, exempt) still previews any method through the private
transport, and **that exemption is self-approvable**: one operator can set `allow_in_preview` on a draft and then fire a
`POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH` or `DELETE` with no second person, no proposal, no lease and no receipt (it is audited). The reference
profile does not close that yet; making preview read-only there is #1072. The callers of the
public entry are pinned by `tests/test_effect_path_matrix.py::test_the_raw_openapi_executor_is_named_only_by_pinned_callers`, so a
new one fails until it is routed or pinned with a reason.

**Configuration, migration and rollback.** No new setting, no route and no migration. The two names `openapi_http` and
`openapi-http` become reserved tool names like the other connectors (`409 reserved_tool_name`); a tool already registered
under one is untrusted and unaffected. Reverting the change restores the direct call (a proposal already recorded remains
readable).

## Memory is owned, derived and read-mostly

Until the owned memory lifecycle (M20: retention, legal hold, deletion) exists, the reference profile does not offer
free-form durable memory (B12 memory, #667). The `/memory` API and the in-run memory tools behave as follows:

- **No free-form partition.** `agent_id` must name an agent or workflow, and `run_id` a workflow run, that the caller
  can see; `user_id` must be the caller's own identity, admins included. A scope value that is present but not a
  non-empty string is a `400`, not ignored. A run id alone is refused (`403`).
- **The partition is pinned to the caller.** With an `agent_id`, the memory is the caller's own within that agent or
  workflow (the server adds `user_id`); with none, it is the caller's own namespace, qualified by the active
  project (`<project>:<user>`). A client never chooses whose memory a read or write reaches, and `metadata` may not
  carry `user_id`, `agent_id`, `run_id` or `actor_id` (`400`), because mem0 filters on those stored fields.
- **One refusal, no disclosure.** A partition that does not exist, one that belongs to another project or user, and a
  label that names nothing all answer `404 memory partition not found`; no id is echoed.
- **Writes are verbatim.** `POST /memory` requires `infer=false` (`403` otherwise), because LLM-inferred writes create
  durable facts nobody owns; and startup refuses `CALIBER_MEMORY_INFER=true` while memory is enabled (table above).
- **No bulk deletion.** `DELETE /memory` answers `403`: deleting memory needs the lifecycle's retention and legal-hold
  rules.
- **Bounded reads.** `top_k` is capped at 100.
- **In-run tools.** `memory_search`, `memory_add`, `memory_list` and `list_entities` act on the run initiator's
  memory within the workflow (the initiator is set by the server, never by the model); a run with no initiator gets no
  memory tools.
- **Same rules below the route.** The service layer refuses bulk delete, inferred writes, run-only partitions and
  partition keys in `metadata` (`MemoryLifecycleUnavailableError`). It does not itself check that an `agent_id` or
  `user_id` belongs to the caller: the route and the in-run tool binding do that and are the only callers.

The development profile keeps the previous behaviour. The service uses mem0 2.x's supported scope contract for
search and list: entity identifiers are passed in the `filters` mapping, not as top-level arguments. `add` and
`delete_all` retain mem0's entity-keyword API, while `list_entities` already passes its scope as `filters`. This
keeps the installed mem0 release and the service wrapper on the same boundary without changing the reference
profile's ownership or lifecycle refusals.

## Trace payload visibility in review surfaces

Reference-profile trace visibility and trace-payload visibility are separate decisions. A caller may see a trace or a
review queue without being allowed to read request, response, span input, span output, or governed trace attributes.
For a project-owned experiment, the current project owner and editor roles may read those payloads; viewers and
reviewers do not. An administrator without membership in the owning project is not an implicit payload reader.

The observability trace detail route and the review-queue alignment-example route use the same fail-closed contract:
non-payload identifiers, status, timing, review question answers, provenance, and assessment identifiers remain, while
governed request/response values are replaced with stable `[redacted:<field>]` placeholders. The queue detail route
itself contains item identifiers and review metadata only; it does not grant payload access.

`POST /eval-datasets/{dataset_id}/examples/from-trace` first resolves trace identity and visibility without mapping
payloads. It then requires `trace.payload.read` before copying the source request or response. A visible trace without
that permission receives `403`, a foreign or unknown trace receives the same `404` as a missing trace, and neither
refusal changes the dataset version or inserts an example. Supplying explicit `input` or `expected` values does not
bypass the source-trace authorization check. An authorized example records the `from-trace` and source trace tags.

The development profile retains its earlier behavior; these payload gates are part of the reference-profile contract.

## Governed effect spans: the ids that link a trace to its rows (B11.3a, #737)

A governed effect crosses four persisted records: the effect **proposal**, the policy **decision** that authorised the
run, the runtime **approval** that was consumed, and the **effect** itself, which is its verified receipt. The spans of
that path name those rows, so an operator can go from a trace to the database without reading any payload. The module is
`caliber.observability.span_attributes`; B11.3b (#745) reads the same attributes back as a causal chain.

| Span (type) | Opened by | Attributes it can carry |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `effect.approval.commit_check` (`CHAIN`) | `approval_valid_at_commit` | `caliber.proposal_id` once the locked proposal is read; `caliber.approval_id` once the request is bound to that proposal's exact intent, policy and evidence; `caliber.decision_id` from the run's current policy decision, only when every check passed |
| `effect.dispatch` (`TOOL`) | `dispatch` | `caliber.proposal_id` from the proposal read; `caliber.approval_id` and `caliber.decision_id` from the validator's answer; `caliber.effect_id` after the settlement has committed |
| `effect.receipt.write` (`CHAIN`) | `record_receipt` | `caliber.proposal_id`; the proposal's recorded approval (`caliber.approval_id` for an exact-intent approval, `caliber.decision_id` for a policy decision); `caliber.effect_id` once the receipt is stored in the caller's transaction |

`run_tags(ctx, node_id=..., proposal_id=..., decision_id=..., approval_id=..., effect_id=...)` accepts the same four
ids for a caller that has read them from a row, and emits each as `caliber.<name>` only when given.

**An id is a link only if a row backs it.** An attribute is absent, never blank or guessed, when the platform has not
read that row: a proposal that never reached a verified receipt has no `caliber.effect_id` (`unknown` and `failed`
included), the receipt-write span has no `caliber.decision_id` for an exact-intent approval (the proposal row does not
store it), and the approval id a caller passes to `dispatch` is a claim until the validator has bound it to the
proposal, so a refused dispatch never carries it. `caliber.effect_id` is the **receipt id**: the platform's only record
that the downstream effect happened and was read back.

**What can reach a span.** Four keys, one allow-list, no payload:

- Only the four keys above, `caliber.refusal_code` and the tracer's own `caliber.status`, `caliber.error_type` and
  `caliber.error` are set on these spans. No URL, argument, request, response, scope, approver, evidence hash or
  exception message is ever an attribute.
- A value must be a plain string that is an opaque identifier: ASCII letters, digits, `.`, `_`, `:`, `-`, starting
  with a letter, at most 128 characters. Anything else (a number, an email address, whitespace, a path, a longer
  string) is **dropped, not truncated**: a truncated id would name a different row.
- A workflow manifest cannot assert a link. Its `mlflow.trace_group_tags` are merged into the run tags first, and the
  five reserved keys are removed from them, so a tag named `caliber.proposal_id` is ignored.
- A failure inside one of these spans is recorded as the exception *type* and, only when it is a platform refusal
  (`ProposalError`, `EffectRefused`, `ApprovalCommitRefused`), its stable `caliber.refusal_code` such as
  `stale_version`; the `code` of any other exception is not copied. The exception is re-raised after the span has
  closed, so MLflow's own exception event, which keeps the message, never sees it **on these three spans**. The
  re-raised exception still passes through any enclosing span (the workflow node span, `trace_run`), where MLflow
  records its message as it did before this change.
- Tracing never changes the outcome of an effect: a redactor or tracer failure while setting one of these attributes is
  logged at debug level and the attribute is absent (the value is never sent unredacted).

**Who can see them.** The ids, `caliber.refusal_code` and the existing run, node and job ids are on
`profile.SAFE_SPAN_ATTRIBUTES`, so a caller who may see a trace but not read its payload (B11.4b, above) sees them; every
other span attribute stays `[redacted:attributes.<key>]`, which includes `caliber.error`. An id does not widen who can
open a trace: the trace, and then the row, still follow experiment and project visibility. `caliber.approval_id` is also
the name of an existing *release* tag (`AP-...`, a prompt-version approval, see the prompts architecture page); on these
spans it is always a runtime approval (`RAP-...`), told apart by the span name.

**Refusal and recovery, with exact examples.**

- *A stale approval.* The recheck finds the resource moved on. The `effect.approval.commit_check` span has
  `caliber.proposal_id`, `caliber.approval_id`, `caliber.refusal_code = stale_version` and `caliber.status = failed`, and no
  `caliber.decision_id`; `effect.dispatch` has `caliber.proposal_id` and the same code. Nothing was sent, the approval is
  unconsumed and the proposal is still `proposed`. Recovery: request a new approval for the current resource version.
- *An approval id that is not this run's.* The recheck answers `not_found`; no span carries that id, only the proposal
  (read from the row) and the code. Recovery: use the id returned when the request was created.
- *A lease lost after the effect was sent.* `effect.dispatch` has the proposal, approval and decision (the claim had
  committed), `caliber.refusal_code = lease_lost` and no `caliber.effect_id`; no receipt exists and the proposal stays
  `dispatched`. Recovery is unchanged: the reconciler asks the downstream by key under the new lease.
- *An answer nobody could verify* (an ambiguous transport result, or a 2xx the downstream's own query did not confirm).
  The proposal becomes `unknown`; `effect.dispatch` completes without `caliber.effect_id`. A missing effect id is the
  signal, not an error.

**Not covered, said plainly.** The node span of a workflow run does not carry these ids (the dispatcher's own spans do, and the same ids are in the
database); the legacy effect-ledger path used
by a plan with no governed context emits none; and the receipt-write span describes a *write*: if the caller's
transaction is rolled back afterwards, the dispatch span, which names the effect only after commit, is the authority.
Tracing is inert unless MLflow is installed and tracing is enabled, and an exporter failure never changes what the effect
does.

**Configuration, migration and rollback.** No new setting, no migration and no stored data change. The spans open inside
the transaction that holds the approval locks, but make no database call of their own. Rolling
back is reverting the change; traces already recorded keep their attributes.

### Reading the links back: `GET /workflow-runs/{run_id}/causal-links` (B11.3b, #745)

The spans above name rows; this endpoint returns the rows. It answers, for one run, with the persisted records that
connect it to its governed effects, **by id, digest, state and timestamp only**, so a reviewer (or the evidence package
of B14) can follow `run -> manifest -> step context -> proposal -> approval -> decision -> receipt` without reading a
payload. It is read-only and is implemented by `caliber.observability.causal_links` (`read_causal_links`), which takes an
already-authorized run row and never an id from a request.

**Who may call it.** The same access as reading the run (a run you cannot see is `404`) **plus** a role in the run's
project (`read`: viewer, reviewer, editor or owner), evaluated on every request from the caller's current membership. A
caller who can see the run but has no role in its project, a caller from another project, a platform administrator with
no project role (`caliber.admin` is not a project role) and an unknown id all get the **same `404`**
(`workflow run '<id>' not found`), and a malformed parameter from such a caller is also that `404`, never a `400`. Nothing
in the query string (a project, a second run id) widens access. A run with no project is gated by its workflow's
visibility alone, as the admission manifest is.

**Sections and paging.** `section` is `effects` (the default), `context_manifests` or `policy_decisions`; only that list
is filled and the other two are `[]`. `limit` is 1 to 200 (default 50). `cursor` is the opaque `next_cursor` of the
previous page (the id of its last row); while `has_more` is true pass it back. Pages are keyset pages ordered by
`(timestamp, id)`, so rows that share a timestamp are neither skipped nor repeated, and a cursor that names no row of this
run, or is not one this API issued, is `400 cursor is invalid` (a cursor from another run opens nothing). A page costs a
fixed number of queries (the run manifest, the page, and one lookup each for contexts, approvals, decisions and receipts),
not one per effect.

**What an effect shows.** For each proposal: `proposal_id`, `node_id`, `occurrence_id`, `node_step_id`, `state`,
`connector`, `connector_version`, `effect_class`, `intent_hash` and the two timestamps, then four links, each with a
`status` and, when it is not simply `linked`, a stable `code`. The statuses: `linked` (a row of this run), `not_required` (the record shows the link is not on this effect's path), `pending` (the effect is still in flight, so the row is expected to appear), `missing` (the chain needs a row, the effect is settled or the stored id names nothing, and there is none: **a broken chain**) and `unrecorded` (the platform does not store this link against the effect, so it can be neither followed nor called broken). In-flight work is never `missing`:

| Link | `linked` | Other statuses and codes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `context_manifest` | the latest context manifest of this node occurrence (highest attempt, then highest revision), by id, revision, attempt and digest | `unrecorded` / `no_context_manifest_for_node_step` (a step that is not an agent step has none, and the proposal does not say which kind of step it came from, so its absence is neither followable nor proven broken) |
| `approval` | an exact-intent approval request the proposal records, bound to this proposal in this run: ids, digests, request status, `superseded_by`, requested, decided, expires and consumed timestamps | `not_required` / `approved_by_policy_decision`; `pending` / `approval_not_consumed` (a request exists but the dispatcher has not consumed it; its id and status are shown), `approval_not_requested`; `not_required` / `failed_before_approval` (settled `failed` with no approval ever recorded); `missing` / `approval_row_missing` (the stored approval id names no row bound to this proposal in this run) |
| `decision` | the policy decision a *policy-approved read* records: id, action, result, reason codes, policy version, input hash, evaluated-at | `unrecorded` / `decision_recorded_per_run_only` (exact-intent approvals, below); `pending` / `not_approved_yet`; `not_required` / `failed_before_approval`; `missing` / `decision_row_missing` |
| `effect` | the verified receipt: `effect_id` (the receipt id, **the id `caliber.effect_id` carries**), attempt, receipt and response digests, verified-at, and `committed` (true when the proposal records that receipt as the one that settled it) | `pending` with `not_dispatched`, `outcome_pending`, `outcome_unknown` or `reconciled_without_receipt`, by the proposal's state (the effect is not settled); `not_required` / `failed_without_receipt` (settled `failed`: nothing was verified and nothing will be); `missing` / `receipt_row_missing` (settled `committed`, which requires a receipt, but no receipt row is there) |

`missing_links` lists only the `missing` links (a broken chain) and `unrecorded_links` the `unrecorded` ones, so a
complete chain (`missing_links == []`) is distinguishable from a broken one, and a healthy exact-intent effect has
`missing_links == []` with `unrecorded_links` naming `decision` (and `context_manifest` for a non-agent step). **An absent
`effect_id` is the marker for an effect that has no verified receipt**, in the API as on the span; it is never filled in
from a neighbouring row, a timestamp or the proposal's state.

`span_attributes` is the `caliber.*` attribute map that the effect's resolved rows support, built by the same allow-list
function (`causal_attributes`). It is a **derived union, not what any one span carries**: each span binds only the ids it
had read when it closed (the receipt span binds the proposal's recorded approval ref even if that row is gone, and the
dispatch span carries the commit-time `decision_id`, which is not persisted against the effect and so is not listed
here). An id is listed only when its row resolved for this run. Nothing is read from the tracing backend, so it cannot
confirm that a trace was exported.

**Digests.** `manifest_digest` (run and context manifests), `receipt_digest` and a policy decision's `input_hash` are bare
lowercase SHA-256 hex (64 characters). `intent_hash`, `evidence_hash`, `policy_digest` and `response_digest` are
`sha256:`-prefixed (71 characters). They are stored in those forms and returned unchanged; compare like with like.

**The decision of an exact-intent approval is not stored against the effect.** The commit-time check records a run
decision (`resource.execute` on `workflow:<id>`, the run authority) and the dispatch span names it, but the proposal row stores only the
approval id, so for an exact-intent effect `decision` is `unrecorded` and its `caliber.decision_id` is not in
`span_attributes`. That decision *is* persisted, per run: `section=policy_decisions` lists the run's decisions
(`decision_id`, `grant_id`, `action`, `resource`, `result`, `reason_codes`, `policy_version`, `input_hash`,
`evaluated_at`), so the `caliber.decision_id` on a span can be checked against a row, but nothing says which effect asked.
Persisting the pairing needs its own migration and must not touch the proposal's frozen columns (follow-up #1061); this
endpoint does not guess it. **Until #1061 lands, a consumer such as the evidence package (B14.1, #818) should treat
`decision: unrecorded` on an exact-intent effect as "run authority asserted per run only": include the run's
`policy_decisions` section in the package and do not fail the chain or invent a pairing.**

**Whole-run markers.** `run_manifest` is `linked` (id, schema version, digest, creation time; the manifest body stays at
`/admission-manifest`), `legacy` (`legacy_run_has_no_manifest`: a run admitted before manifests has none and never will)
or `missing` (`manifest_row_missing`: an admitted run whose row is not there). `acceptance` and `evidence_package` are
`{status: not_available, code: acceptance_record_not_available | evidence_package_not_available}`: those records
(B09, B14) do not exist yet and are never synthesized. `trace_id` is the run's stored trace id, a pointer only.

**What it never returns.** No prompt, argument, intent body, `resource` of a proposal, resource version, downstream request
id, manifest or context body, `requested_by` / `decided_by` / `subject_user_id`, decision prose or policy purpose. The
queries select only the columns above, and the response schema (`CausalLinksSchema`) forbids any other field, so a column
added to a table cannot reach a caller by accident. Connector and node names are manifest- and registry-defined
identifiers and are shown; a policy decision's `resource` is the platform identifier the decision was asked about
(`workflow:<id>`, `effect:<proposal id>`). Every lookup by an id stored on a row is also filtered by the run and, for an
approval, by the proposal, so a stored id that names another run's row is reported `missing`, not followed.

**Refusal and recovery, with exact examples.**

- *Another project's run, or a run that does not exist:* `GET /workflow-runs/WR-1/causal-links` is `404`
  `{"detail": "workflow run 'WR-1' not found"}` for both. Recovery: ask a member of the run's project, or check the id.
- *A removed project member:* `404` from the next request, whatever they could read a moment ago. Recovery: restore the role.
- *`?section=payloads`:* `400 section must be one of effects, context_manifests, policy_decisions`. *`?limit=500`:*
  `400 limit must be between 1 and 200`. *A cursor kept from another run or a tampered one:* `400 cursor is invalid`;
  start again without `cursor`.
- *A proposal with `effect.status = pending` and `code = outcome_unknown`:* the downstream's answer could not be verified.
  There is no `effect_id` to find; the reconciler asks the downstream by key (see **Reconciler** below). Reading this
  endpoint does nothing to it.

**Consistency.** A page is assembled from a handful of reads in one request, not from one snapshot: an effect being
dispatched while you read can show an approval as `pending` and its effect as `pending`, and a later read shows both
linked. A link that appears is always a row that exists; none is ever inferred.

**SDK, configuration and rollback.** `client.workflows.runs.causal_links(run_id, section=, limit=, cursor=)` (sync) and
`client.workflows.causal_links(...)` (async) return a typed `CausalLinks` page (`CausalEffect`, `CausalContextManifest`,
`CausalPolicyDecision` and the link models are in `caliber_sdk.models`); an unknown field is kept in `extra` and a missing
`status` decodes as `None`, never as `linked`. No new setting, no migration, no stored data change; the endpoint is a
read, so rolling back is reverting the change.

## A configuration that passes

```ini
CALIBER_PROFILE=reference
CALIBER_DATABASE_URL=postgresql+psycopg://caliber:CHANGE_ME@db.internal:5432/caliber
CALIBER_AUTH_MODE=session
CALIBER_AUTH_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD_ENV=CALIBER_BOOTSTRAP_PASSWORD
CALIBER_AUTH_BOOTSTRAP_ALLOW_INSECURE_DEFAULT=false
CALIBER_AUTH_DEV_FALLBACK_ENABLED=false
CALIBER_ADMIN_USERS=admin
CALIBER_APPROVER_USERS=approver
CALIBER_CSRF_ENABLED=true
CALIBER_CSRF_SIGNING_SECRET_ENV=CALIBER_CSRF_SIGNING_SECRET
CALIBER_EGRESS_POLICY_ENABLED=true
CALIBER_MCP_ALLOW_INSECURE_HTTP=false
CALIBER_APPROVAL_ALLOW_SELF_APPROVAL=false
CALIBER_APPLY_REQUIRE_DISTINCT_APPROVER=true
```

Two of the variables name *other* variables that hold secrets (`CALIBER_BOOTSTRAP_PASSWORD` and
`CALIBER_CSRF_SIGNING_SECRET`); set those in your secret store, not in this file. What happens when they are
missing differs, and neither case is a profile refusal:

- **No CSRF signing secret:** with CSRF on, the server refuses to boot (a `RuntimeError`, not the profile's
  `ConfigError`). That check runs *after* the database is opened and the bootstrap account is written, so unlike
  a profile refusal it can leave those behind.
- **No bootstrap password:** the server **starts** and logs a warning, but nobody can sign in.
- **No role lists:** `CALIBER_ADMIN_USERS`, `CALIBER_OPERATOR_USERS` and `CALIBER_APPROVER_USERS` default to
  empty, and the bootstrap account is then a viewer that cannot create projects; the server logs an error. The
  example names an admin and an approver. Because self-approval is refused, an approver must be a different
  account from whoever starts a run.

The database must be migrated (`caliber-migrate`) before the first start.

## Migrations that shipped in the alpha never change

An alpha database sits at the head of the migrations that `caliber-v0.1.0a1` shipped; upgrading it means running
the migrations after that head. That is only safe while the migrations up to that head are exactly the ones the
alpha ran, so they are frozen (B16-Upgrade.1, #702). `caliber/tests/fixtures/alpha_0_1_0a1_migration_checksums.json`
records the SHA-256 of every migration file in the tag, read from the tag's objects, together with the tag's commit,
the alpha head and the alembic version table (`caliber_alembic_version`). The head is derived from those files (the
one revision nothing revises), never written in by hand.

Two checks guard it, because each alone can be defeated:

- `caliber/tests/test_upgrade_from_alpha.py::test_shipped_migrations_unchanged` compares the working tree with the
  manifest. It needs no history, so it runs everywhere and never skips. It fails if a migration is edited (a
  line-ending change counts), renamed or removed, or if one is inserted into or branched off the shipped history.
  A change that edits a migration *and* its manifest entry passes it.
- `test_the_manifest_matches_the_release_tag` (and `python caliber/tests/migration_checksums.py generate --check`)
  regenerates the manifest from the tag and compares, which fails that change. The backend-core CI job fetches the
  tag and sets `CALIBER_REQUIRE_ALPHA_TAG=1`, so there a missing tag is a failure, not a skip; elsewhere the test
  skips when neither the tag nor its commit is in the checkout. `.github/CODEOWNERS` also sends any change to the
  migrations directory or the manifest to the owner.

Migrations added after the alpha are fine as long as they descend from the alpha head, and they need no manifest
update. Each failure names the file and the way out, for example:

```text
0050_assistant_attachments.py: changed since caliber-v0.1.0a1 (sha256 6c27..., shipped 4306...). Restore it from the
shipped commit (`git show 3f3b562...:caliber/src/caliber/db/migrations/versions/0050_assistant_attachments.py > ...`,
from the repository root) and put the change in a new migration that revises the current head.
```

A changed or missing file is restored from the recorded commit (the command is in the message and does not depend on
the tag name being present). A new migration that revises a shipped revision is re-parented onto the current head
(`alembic heads`). `python caliber/tests/migration_checksums.py verify` runs the working-tree check from the command
line. Regenerate the manifest (`... migration_checksums.py generate`, with the tag fetched) only if the fixture itself
was wrong.

`.gitattributes` marks the migrations `-text`, so a Windows checkout with `core.autocrlf=true` cannot rewrite their
line endings (the checksums are of exact bytes).

For the alpha-upgrade tests that follow (#708, #715): create the alpha database by running `alembic upgrade
<alpha head>` through the working-tree migrations directory, with the manifest's `version_table`. That reproduces the
alpha schema only because those files are frozen, which the never-skipping check enforces. Never read the migrations
from the tag in CI; it is not in the checkout.

### The seeded alpha database (B16-Upgrade.2, #708)

`caliber/tests/alpha_seed.py` builds a database an alpha operator could really have, for the upgrade test that
follows (#715). It is an offline test fixture, not an operator bootstrap path.

- **Schema.** `alembic upgrade <alpha head>` through the working-tree migrations (the head and the version table come
  from the manifest above). Before migrating, it re-verifies that the migration directory alembic reads is
  byte-identical to the manifest, so the schema built is the alpha's. Nothing is read from the tag.
- **Data.** Raw `INSERT` statements from literals in the file, using the alpha table and column names, not
  `caliber.db.models`. Every row lists every column, so no value comes from a database default or a clock: the same
  bytes on every run, on SQLite and on PostgreSQL 16. 35 tables, 140 rows: three users (one disabled), three projects
  (one archived) with their environments and members, a session and access tokens, workflows with published and draft
  versions and deployments, nine runs in every status (including `running` and `waiting_approval`), their events and
  checkpoints, runtime approvals, effect-ledger rows `in_progress` (two, unresolved), `completed` and `failed`, a
  workflow service and token, secrets as ciphertext with the tool that references one, a skill, an eval dataset and
  run, a prompt refinement loop (prompt text lives in MLflow, not in this database), audit rows and runtime tables.
  Every hash and ciphertext derives from a public constant; the users' login phrase is `ALPHA_SEED_PASSWORD`.
  `seed_sha256()` fingerprints the data and is pinned in the test.
- **For #715.** `alpha_database(dialect, tmp_path, name)` yields a created and seeded database; `migrate_database(url)`
  upgrades it; `read_seeded_rows(url)` against `expected_rows()` (per table; a table the upgrade rewrites needs its own
  assertion), `row_counts()` and `schema_shape(url)` (compare with a fresh install) check the result.

It fails loudly instead of seeding the wrong database, with `AlphaSeedError`:

```text
not a caliber-v0.1.0a1 database: it records <revision> in caliber_alembic_version, the alpha head is <alpha head>
caliber_projects already holds 3 row(s); seed an unseeded alpha database
the migrations alembic reads are not the ones caliber-v0.1.0a1 shipped, so the schema built from them would not be the alpha's
```

Recovery: use a new, empty database (the fixture creates it); a wrong revision means something migrated it past or
short of the alpha head; the third message means a shipped migration changed, so restore it as described above.

```sh
PYTHONPATH=caliber/src caliber/.venv/bin/python -m pytest caliber/tests/test_upgrade_from_alpha.py
```

The `postgresql` cases run in the "Migration parity (PostgreSQL)" CI job (`CALIBER_TEST_POSTGRES_URL`, the
`pgvector/pgvector:pg16` image, because migration 0060 needs the `vector` extension).

The upgrade proof is `test_alpha_database_upgrades_to_head` in
`caliber/tests/test_upgrade_from_alpha.py`. For each available dialect it migrates the seeded alpha database to the
single current Alembic head, compares every seeded row and the complete reflected schema with a fresh head database,
and verifies that historical workflow runs remain explicitly `manifest_legacy` with no invented runtime lineage. The
two unresolved `in_progress` effect-ledger rows remain visible with no completion timestamp. The same test then uses
the current workflow API to create and publish a new workflow and submit a governed run, proving that the upgraded
database supports new admission without rewriting historical data. SQLite runs locally; PostgreSQL 16 runs when
`CALIBER_TEST_POSTGRES_URL` is configured in the migration-parity job. A failed upgrade must be restored from a fresh
database and investigated before retrying; the test does not attempt an automatic rollback of an operator database.

## A stored secret never leaves the platform

`caliber/tests/test_secret_canary.py` (B12.5b, #666) stores `EGI_CANARY_<uuid4>` as `egi-canary` through the
encrypted secret store, points `llm_api_key_env` at `secret://egi-canary`, and runs the core journey over HTTP with
logging at DEBUG: sign in (the trusted proxy header), create a project, register an agent, publish, promote and run
a workflow, run a **calibration run** to a candidate and **apply** it, read the LLM provider status (which resolves
the secret inside the request; the test fails if nothing in the journey did), and export the audit log, plus refused
requests. It fails if the value appears in any response (status, headers, cookies, body; the helper calls too), any
log record (message, arguments, `extra` fields as the JSON formatter renders them, traceback), any
`caliber_workflow_run_events` row or any audit row. The failure paths of resolution (a revoked secret, corrupted
ciphertext, a provider built from a revoked secret) are scanned the same way, and a control test plants the value in
every scanned surface to prove the scan can fail. It runs in the Backend core job and the full backend suite.

Not covered: the prompt *registry* routes and MLflow traces need a live MLflow registry, which ordinary CI does
not have; the journey's prompts are the agent prompts in the workflow manifest, which the calibration run rewrites.
Sign-in by session login is covered by `test_auth_sessions`, not by this journey.

Running it found that `CALIBER_LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG` with the default S3 log sink recursed: the S3 client's own DEBUG
records re-entered the handler, so each record caused a growing number of S3 writes. The handler now ignores records
emitted while it delivers a batch.

## Run manifests are written once

Migration `0114` adds `caliber_run_manifests` (B02.1a, #656): one row per workflow run holding the canonical
manifest bytes (`manifest_bytes`) and their SHA-256 (`manifest_digest`). The row is immutable:

- a database trigger refuses `UPDATE` and `DELETE` on SQLite and PostgreSQL (PostgreSQL also refuses `TRUNCATE`),
  so a bulk SQL statement fails as well as an ORM one: `caliber_run_manifests is immutable: UPDATE refused`;
- the ORM raises `ImmutableRecordError` before any SQL for an instance update or delete and for an ORM
  `update()`/`delete()` statement (`Session.bulk_*_mappings` and Core/raw SQL skip the ORM and are refused by the
  trigger instead);
- a second manifest for the same run violates `uq_run_manifest_run`, and a digest that is not the SHA-256 of the
  bytes is refused (by the ORM everywhere, and by a CHECK on PostgreSQL).

**Runtime role.** The migration revokes `UPDATE`, `DELETE` and `TRUNCATE` on the table from `PUBLIC`. That only
protects a deployment that runs the application as a role other than the table's owner, and `caliber-migrate`,
`scripts/install.sh` and the shipped compose files use one database URL for both, so by default the application
*is* the owner and is held only by the triggers and the ORM guard. For the privilege layer, run `caliber-migrate`
as the owner and the application as a role granted only what it needs:

```sql
GRANT SELECT, INSERT ON caliber_run_manifests TO caliber_runtime;
GRANT SELECT ON caliber_workflow_runs TO caliber_runtime;  -- already held; the insert trigger reads it
-- no UPDATE, DELETE or TRUNCATE on caliber_run_manifests; avoid ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES ... GRANT ALL
```

A trigger can be disabled by the table's owner or by a session with `session_replication_role = replica`; only the
missing privilege holds against the runtime role. The reference profile does **not** check which role the
application connects as (listed under "Not enforced yet"). The trigger functions are pinned to the migration's
schema with `pg_temp` last in `search_path`, so a temporary table cannot shadow `caliber_workflow_runs`.

**Legacy runs.** `caliber_workflow_runs.manifest_legacy` is `true` by default, so every run that existed when `0114`
ran, and every run created by a path other than admission, is legacy. Such a run has no manifest and can never get
one (`a manifest needs an existing, non-legacy run`, also raised for a run that does not exist), and the flag
cannot be changed afterwards (`caliber_workflow_runs.manifest_legacy is write-once`), so a historical pin cannot be
fabricated. Admission (#680, below) creates a run with `manifest_legacy = false` in the same transaction as its
manifest. A client with `DELETE` on runs can still delete a legacy run and re-insert the same id as a non-legacy
one; that needs write access to runs and is not guarded here.

**Retention and deletion.** A run that has a manifest is retained evidence: retention pruning
(`CALIBER_WORKFLOW_RUN_RETENTION_DAYS`) skips it, and `DELETE /workflows/{id}` answers `409`
(`cannot delete workflow: its runs have immutable run manifests`) while any of its runs has one, because removing
the run would either violate the manifest's foreign key (PostgreSQL) or orphan it (SQLite). Legacy and
manifest-less runs are pruned and deleted as before. Rolling the schema back past 0113 drops the table
and therefore the manifests, never the runs; upgrading again starts with no manifests and marks every existing run
legacy.

### Reading a run's manifest (B02.5, #695)

Two endpoints, two different manifests; neither changes the other.

| endpoint | what it returns |
| --- | --- |
| `GET /workflow-runs/{run_id}/manifest` (unchanged) | the **workflow** manifest the run executed: `workflow_run_id`, `workflow_id`, `workflow_version_id`, `manifest_mode`, `manifest_hash`, `manifest`. Served for every run, legacy included. |
| `GET /workflow-runs/{run_id}/admission-manifest` (new) | the run's immutable **admission** manifest: `workflow_run_id`, `schema_version`, `legacy`, `manifest_id`, `run_manifest` (the stored record verbatim: pins, subject, workload, purpose, scope, grant id, request digest) and `manifest_digest` (the SHA-256 of its canonical bytes, so a reader can check it). |

The new endpoint needs the same access as reading the run (a run you cannot see is `404`, indistinguishable from a
missing one) **plus** a role in the run's project (`read`): a caller who can see a run, for example through a public
workflow, but has no role in its project also gets that same `404`, never the project's name. A run with no project is
gated by the workflow's visibility alone. A **legacy** run (admission was off, or a path that is not admitted)
answers `200` with `legacy: true` and `schema_version`, `manifest_id`, `run_manifest` and `manifest_digest` all `null`:
no history is fabricated. An admitted run whose stored manifest does not read back, is missing or is not in
canonical form (so its digest could not be checked) is `409` (`manifest_corrupt` / `manifest_missing`). The SDK has
`client.workflows.runs.admission_manifest(run_id)` (sync) and `client.workflows.admission_manifest(run_id)` (async),
returning an `AdmissionManifest` (`legacy` is `None`, never "admitted", when the server did not say); the console API
client has `getWorkflowRunAdmissionManifest`. `run_manifest` is the stored record verbatim, so it carries the
subject's user id, the grant id, the request digest and, when a rule bundle is pinned, **its absolute server path**:
treat the endpoint as project-member-visible evidence.

### Building a manifest (admission, #676)

`caliber/src/caliber/run_manifest.py` turns *resolved* inputs into the manifest record and its canonical bytes. It is
a pure function: no SQL, clock, randomness or provider call, so the same input always gives the same bytes and digest.
It does not choose or persist the manifest (admission, #680 and #684, does); the caller stores
`BuiltManifest.row_values()` with `CaliberRunManifest`.

```python
pinned = pin_rule_bundle(path, expected_sha256)          # only when rule bundles are enabled; reads the file once
built = build_run_manifest(
    manifest_id=new_manifest_id(), workflow_run_id=run_id, pins=ResolvedPins(...),
    subject=Subject(...), workload=Workload.for_workflow(name, digest), purpose="...",
    scope=DeploymentScope.fixed(project_id), created_at=now_utc,
    rule_bundle=pinned, rule_bundles_enabled=True,
)
```

- **Resolved, never named.** Every pin must be the concrete value the run will use, and resolving it is the
  caller's duty: the builder cannot see the database, so it rejects what it can *recognise* as a moving target. After
  Unicode (NFKC) folding, a segment that is a floating word (`latest`, `current`, `head`, `default`, `stable`, `main`,
  `master`, `nightly`, ... as in `v-latest` or `gpt-4o-latest`), a wildcard version segment (`1.x`) or a range or
  wildcard character (`*`, `^`, `>=`, `${...}`) is `unresolved_pin`; a prompt, tool or skill pin is exactly
  `<name>@<version>` and only the version is checked; `bundle_digest` is a full lowercase SHA-256. Strings must be
  NFC, at most 512 characters (64 for the manifest and run ids), and lists at most 256 entries. Lists are sorted and may not repeat
  (`duplicate_pin`), so the order of resolution never changes the digest. A manifest is never filled in later.
- **Fixed scope.** `DeploymentScope` carries organization (`tenant_id`), project, region and residency, all
  server-derived and **enforced**: the builder refuses (`bad_scope`) a scope whose organization, region or residency
  is not the deployment's (`local` in the reference profile, ADR 0001). A caller that names another organization is
  `organization_switch`; a subject acting in another project than the run's scope is `project_mismatch`. The
  manifest records `project_id` (optional in the v1 schema, absent for a run outside any project).
- **Rule bundle.** When rule bundles are enabled the bundle is loaded and verified first (`pin_rule_bundle`, #726): a
  missing, oversized, changed or malformed file, or one whose context-manifest citation would exceed 256 KiB (see "The
  rule bundle at context use"), is `rule_bundle_refused` and no manifest is built; a verified bundle's
  symlink-resolved absolute path and SHA-256 are recorded (make one `PinnedRuleBundle` per admission: it is a snapshot, not a handle on the file). Enabled without one is `rule_bundle_required`; one given while disabled is
  `rule_bundle_unexpected`. The digest in the manifest is the digest of the bytes that were verified, so editing the
  file afterwards changes nothing about this run (the context code re-verifies the bytes when it uses them, #736: see
  "The context manifest", "The rule bundle at context use").
- **The request digest.** `request_digest` (optional, 64 lowercase hex) is the SHA-256 of the canonical admission
  intent (see "Admitting a run"). A malformed one is `bad_pin`. It is part of the sealed bytes, so it cannot change
  after admission.
- **The digest excludes itself.** `manifest_digest` is the SHA-256 of the canonical bytes (sorted keys, no
  whitespace, UTF-8, no `NaN`); the record carries no digest field.
- **Self-consistent result.** `BuiltManifest` re-reads its own bytes on construction (digest, schema, UTF-8, no
  duplicate key or lone surrogate), so bytes and digest cannot disagree; `row_values()` includes `created_at`.
- **Strict writer, tolerant reader.** The builder is stricter than the v1 schema (which takes any non-empty string),
  so records written before it still validate and `read_manifest(bytes, digest)` still reads them.

| code | meaning | recovery |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `unresolved_pin` | a pin is empty, missing or a floating selector | resolve it to a version or digest, then retry |
| `bad_pin` | a pin has the wrong type or shape (for example a digest that is not 64 lowercase hex) | fix the resolver |
| `duplicate_pin` | the same reference twice (a knowledge base may be pinned at several versions, each once) | name each once |
| `bad_scope` | a scope field is empty or not a clean identifier | fix the deployment configuration |
| `organization_switch` | the caller asked for another organization | none: this deployment serves one organization |
| `project_mismatch` | the subject's project is not the run's project | admit the run in the subject's project |
| `bad_field` | manifest id, run id, purpose or timestamp is malformed (a naive datetime) | supply clean values and an aware time |
| `rule_bundle_refused` | the configured bundle's bytes are missing, changed or invalid, or its context citation is over 256 KiB (262144 bytes) | restore the bundle or update the pinned digest deliberately; shorten `source_ref` values or split a bundle that is over the cap |
| `rule_bundle_required` / `rule_bundle_unexpected` | enabled without a verified bundle / a bundle while disabled | align the configuration and the call |
| `invalid_manifest` | stored bytes are not a valid manifest, or do not match their digest (`read_manifest`) | treat as corruption: the row is immutable evidence |

### Admitting a run (B02.2a, #680)

With admission on (always under `CALIBER_PROFILE=reference`, otherwise `CALIBER_ADMISSION_ENABLED=true`), every run a
user *queues* is admitted: the run, its grant, its policy decision and its immutable manifest are created in one
transaction, or none of them are. The paths covered are the create-run route (`POST /workflow-runs`), a retry of a
failed run (`POST /workflow-runs/{id}/retry`, a new run admitted afresh), the event trigger
(`POST /workflows/{id}/trigger`) and the assistant's `run_workflow` tool. The first three authenticate and check
`resource.execute` in the workflow's project *before* admission; the assistant path checks the workflow's visibility
first and the caller's role when the grant is issued (inside the same transaction, with the same outcome). A
synchronous real run (`POST /workflow-versions/{id}/run`) is never queued, so with admission on it is refused
(`409`, `sync_run_not_admitted`): use the queue.

1. **Pins first.** Before any row is written, everything the run depends on is taken from the version's *sealed
   deployment bundle* (prompts, tools, MCP tools, skills, knowledge-base versions, the models its agents name, the
   policy version, the bundle's own digest) and the configured rule bundle is loaded and verified
   (`CALIBER_RULE_BUNDLE_PATH`/`_SHA256`). The manifest is built by [the builder](#building-a-manifest-admission-676).
   A version that was never compiled, whose bundle fails its integrity check, or that has an unresolved runtime
   dependency, is refused (`409`, `bundle_unavailable`); so is a rule bundle that is missing or changed
   (`manifest_refused: rule_bundle_refused`). An unresolved evaluation dataset does not stop a run. **The worker
   executes exactly what the pins describe:** an admitted run's manifest snapshot is the bundle's sealed *resolved*
   manifest (prompts inline, tool versions exact, knowledge-base versions and child workflows resolved), not the
   authoring manifest, so moving a prompt alias after admission changes nothing about the run. (Skills are
   embedded in the bundle's snapshots; embedding and chat models of knowledge nodes are not part of the model
   pins yet.)
2. **One transaction.** The run is inserted with `manifest_legacy = false`, then the grant is issued (never beyond the
   caller's *current* role), the decision is recorded under the policy (`policy-v1`: risk ceiling 4), and only on an
   allow the manifest is stored. A denial (`403`, with the decision's reason codes) or any later failure rolls the
   transaction back: no run, grant, decision, manifest or event remains, and no partial admitted run can be
   dispatched.
3. **Retries.** A request that reuses an idempotency key is authorized first, then returns the *original* run and
   manifest when it is the same request from the same caller (same workflow, release selector, explicit version
   selector, input, files, project, release/environment/model, priority and session) even if the alias has since
   moved, been deactivated or now points at a version that fails a preflight, or the workflow is paused (the key is
   looked up, after the caller is authorized, *before* the target is resolved); any difference, including another caller, is a `409` (`intent_conflict`, one message for every
   difference, so it is not an oracle). "The same request" is the canonical *intent*: the workflow, the selectors as
   named (never what they resolved to), the input, the purpose and the server-derived scope. Its SHA-256 is stored in
   the immutable manifest as `request_digest` and the retry is compared with that, not with anything on the mutable
   run row (the intent itself is also kept in the run's summary for diagnosis; a run admitted before the digest
   existed is compared on its stored intent when that is complete, and is a `409` when it is not; a legacy run is
   compared on the fields its own row keeps). An input that is not text is compared as canonical JSON, so the key
   order of an object does not matter and a string that prints like the object is a different request. A trigger
   names its alias only if the caller did: the intent records what was asked, not the alias the trigger picked. An admitted run whose manifest is
   missing or cannot be read fails the retry closed (`500`, `manifest_refused`). The key's scope is (workflow, source, key), so the same
   key from another source or in another project's workflow is a different request. A key that names a run created while
   admission was off returns that legacy run (it has no manifest). Two requests racing on one key admit exactly one
   run, and the loser gets the same answer a later retry would (PostgreSQL scenario).
4. **Lineage (B02.4, #691).** Under `CALIBER_PROFILE=reference` every run started through the create-run route, the
   event trigger, the cron scheduler or a service token names the workspace release and environment it runs against (`workspace_release_id` and
   `environment_id`, together; optionally `model_id` and `config_sha256`): a run without them is `422` with
   `{"error": "lineage_required"}` before anything is read or written (`run_launch.require_lineage`,
   `LineageRequiredError`), and the run is created with its immutable runtime lineage. A lineage that is not valid for
   the project (unknown or foreign release or environment, a config digest that is not the release's, a release that is
   not eligible) is `409`; a malformed one (empty ids, a digest that is not 64 lowercase hex) is `400`. A **retry**
   keeps the lineage of the run it retries (a fresh lineage record for the new run, refused with `409` if the release is
   no longer eligible) and a run that never had one cannot be retried in the reference profile (`422`). Development
   leaves lineage optional. **Not covered, tracked:** the assistant's run tool (a chat has no release to name) is
   refused with the same code. The console's Run and Trigger actions load the project's active environments and approved
   workspace releases, offer only exact current-release/environment pairs, and submit both IDs. If no eligible pair is
   available, the controls show the same `lineage_required` refusal and do not issue a run or trigger request; the server
   still revalidates project scope, approval and freshness (#968).
5. **Who and what.** A user-started run has the authenticated caller (`session`, `pat` or `trusted_header`) as its
   subject. A scheduler or service-token run has a server-created `service_principal` subject instead:
   `principal_id` is `service_principal:cron:<workflow_id>` for the scheduler or `service_token:<token_id>` for the
   service route. The principal is fixed to the local tenant, workflow project, pinned workload, purpose and allowed
   action/resource set; it carries no ambient user scopes and is not admitted through human project membership. The
   workload is the workflow pinned to its version digest, the purpose is `workflow_run:<path>` with the route's own
   word (`api`, `event`, `retry`, `assistant`, `cron` or `service`), never the
   client-chosen `source` field, and the scope is the fixed
   deployment (`local` organization, region and residency) plus the workflow's project. The caller must be acting in
   the workflow's project, and a credential bound to another project is refused (`403`). A workflow outside any
   project cannot be admitted (`409`, `project_required`); a manifest override on a manual run cannot be pinned, so
   it is not admitted (`409`, `manifest_override_not_admitted`).

| response | code | meaning and recovery |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `422` | `lineage_required` | the reference profile starts no run without runtime lineage: name a `workspace_release_id` and an `environment_id` together (the body is `{"error": "lineage_required", ...}`); nothing was stored |
| `409` | `project_required` | the workflow has no project; move it into one |
| `409` | `bundle_unavailable` | compile and publish the version again (its sealed bundle is missing, altered or unresolved) |
| `409` | `manifest_refused` | a pin is floating or ambiguous, the rule bundle is missing or changed, or the project belongs to another organization; the message says which |
| `409` | `intent_conflict` | the idempotency key belongs to a different request; use a new key |
